newsitem.title: HONG KONG: ASIAN METALS - Lead talked up as contract time nears.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN METALS - Lead talked up as contract time nears.

text.p: Lead traders are talking up their books as the season for negotiating 1997 supply contracts and premiums approaches, Far East metals industry sources said on Monday.
The current lead premium is hovering around US$40 to $50 a tonne over the London Metal Exchange cash price for Western lead, and $75 to $80 on Chinese lead, one Hong Kong trader said.
Another trader with a major international firm, however, quoted premiums at 1995 levels, when supplies were tight and panic among end-users was the order of the day.
He said Western lead was arriving at Southeast Asian ports at premiums of $135 to 145, compared to the premium on Chinese metal of $100 a tonne.
The lead price on the LME moved down US$5 a tonne in Friday trading to $782 a tonne after inventory movements came within market expectations, moving up by 2,950 tonnes to 117,400 tonnes.
Analysts, pointing out a 25 percent fall in LME lead stocks since the start of 1996, have said they see the lead market in deficit as stocks are running down.
The lead negotiating season traditionally begins in late October with Southeast Asian consumers, and in December or January with South Korean and Japanese users, an Australian source said.
"It's a pretty set pattern," he said. "They know by the second half of October that it's time to start talking."
Premiums on pure lead remained non-negotiable for the duration of the negotiated year, he said, while alloy premiums were somewhat flexible.
South Korea, with annual imports of 265,000 tonnes, was fast gaining ground on Japan, which, as the world's biggest importer, takes around 280,000 tonnes a year, he said.
South Korea's massive automobile industry accounted for growth in consumption of 10 to 15 percent a year. Japanese consumption, by contrast, was falling by around one percent a year, he said.
The Chinese market remained a mystery, he said, though annual exports had dropped from 190,000 tonnes three years ago, to around 90,000 tonnes in 1995.
A Singapore trader reported a discernible pick-up in regional demand with the expansion of battery production.
The upward pressure of 1995 had gone, he said, though "there is not a huge excess so the LME price should hold well".
Other metals remained quiet.
The movement of 20,000 tonnes of copper out of Shanghai bonded warehouses, a good proportion of it to Singapore, had had no effect on the market, a trader in Singapore said.

Copper premiums in the Far East had eased from recent highs, to $60-65 a tonne over the LME cash price, with one Singapore trading source seeing long-term support for the per tonne price remaining between $1,800 and $1,900 a tonne.
Aluminium premiums had strengthened to $200 a tonne, the one available aluminium trader said.
"There is not much material in the warehouses," he said. "There is some, but it is in a few hands."
Aluminium producers were having difficulty covering costs, he said, as business that usually kicked in from September 1 had failed to materialise.
"It is a pessimistic picture," he said.
